eu.name: European Union
eu.blurb: Regulates via REACH, CLP, and the Cosmetics Regulation — the world's strictest chemical framework. Often years ahead of US federal action.

uk.name: United Kingdom
uk.blurb: Retained EU chemicals law post-Brexit (UK REACH); continues banning/restricting in lockstep with the EU.

ca.name: Canada
ca.blurb: Health Canada restricts cosmetics/consumer chemicals; lists under CEPA, often ahead of the US.

jp.name: Japan
jp.blurb: CSCL + cosmetics standards; restricts several preservatives and allergens the US allows.

us.name: United States
us.blurb: No federal cosmetics ban list; EPA registration + CA Prop 65 are the main levers. Prop 65 (California) often outruns the FDA.

Methylisothiazolinone.rule: EU Cosmetics Reg. Annex V — 15 ppm max in leave-on products (was 100). Effectively banned in leave-on cosmetics.
Methylisothiazolinone.reason: Epidemic of allergic contact dermatitis — named Contact Allergen of the Year 2013. Dermatology clinics saw mass patch-test spikes from wet wipes and cosmetics.

Methylisothiazolinone.rule: Health Canada aligned with the EU: 15 ppm cap in leave-on cosmetics.
Methylisothiazolinone.reason: Same allergic-contact-dermatitis epidemic, mirrored across North American patch-test data.

Benzisothiazolinone.rule: EU Cosmetics Reg. — rinse-off use only; prohibited in leave-on products; labeled as a sensitizer.
Benzisothiazolinone.reason: Cross-reacting isothiazolinone; occupational contact dermatitis (paints, cleaners) and consumer allergy burden.

Quaternary Ammonium.rule: EU Biocidal Products Regulation — quats (incl. DDAC, BAC) under rolling approval reviews with tightening conditions.
Quaternary Ammonium.reason: Occupational asthma and allergic sensitization studies; aquatic toxicity; overuse concerns post-pandemic.

Didecyldimonium Chloride.rule: EU BPR approval review — DDAC use conditions being tightened.
Didecyldimonium Chloride.reason: Respiratory sensitization in occupational cleaning studies; very toxic to aquatic life (H400).

Benzalkonium Chloride.rule: EU Cosmetics Reg. Annex V — max 0.1% in cosmetics, extra conditions for spray products.
Benzalkonium Chloride.reason: Skin/respiratory sensitization documented in healthcare and cleaning workers (NIOSH n=585 HLA-DP study); repro concerns in animal data.

Butyloxyethanol.rule: EU CLP — classified Reproductive toxicant 1B (H360FD); restricted in consumer products from 2019. Effectively out of EU household cleaners.
Butyloxyethanol.reason: Reproductive/developmental harm evidence (the same class as 2-methoxy/2-ethoxyethanol bans).

Butyloxyethanol.rule: California Prop 65 — listed for reproductive/developmental harm. No federal consumer ban; still sold in US glass cleaners.
Butyloxyethanol.reason: State-level 'catch-up' signal: US federal law never restricted it, so California stepped in.

Fragrance.rule: EU Cosmetics Reg. — mandatory labeling of 26 known fragrance allergens above thresholds; several phthalates (DEHP, DBP, BBP) banned outright in cosmetics.
Fragrance.reason: Contact allergy burden from undisclosed fragrance; endocrine concerns over phthalates. US law treats fragrance as a trade secret — no allergen labeling required.

Limonene.rule: EU — one of the 26 mandatory-labeled fragrance allergens (d-limonene).
Limonene.reason: Oxidizes on exposure to air into potent contact sensitizers (limonene hydroperoxides) — a major allergy source in cleaning products.

Essential Oils.rule: EU — linalool, limonene, geraniol, citral etc. must be labeled when present above thresholds.
Essential Oils.reason: Common sensitizers; consumers deserve to know which specific oils are in 'essential oil' blends.

Sodium Laureth Sulfate.rule: EU — 1,4-dioxane (ethoxylation byproduct, IARC 2B probable carcinogen) restricted as a cosmetic contaminant.
Sodium Laureth Sulfate.reason: SLES is not banned, but the process contaminant 1,4-dioxane is capped. US: no federal limit; CA Prop 65 lists it.

Alcohol Ethoxylates.rule: EU — 1,4-dioxane contaminant monitoring; CLP classification of the byproduct.
Alcohol Ethoxylates.reason: Same ethoxylation byproduct issue as SLES.

Alcohol Ethoxylate.rule: EU — 1,4-dioxane contaminant monitoring; CLP classification of the byproduct.
Alcohol Ethoxylate.reason: Same ethoxylation byproduct issue as SLES.

Phenoxyethanol.rule: EU Cosmetics Reg. — max 1% in cosmetics; additional warnings for use around infants.
Phenoxyethanol.reason: Repro/developmental toxicity signals in animal studies at higher doses.

Hydrogen Peroxide.rule: EU Cosmetics Reg. Annex III — concentration caps by use (e.g., 12% in hair products).

Sodium Tetraborate.rule: EU CLP — Reproductive toxicant 1B (H360FD). Borates restricted in many consumer products; EU banned in cosmetic leave-on.
Sodium Tetraborate.reason: Reproductive/developmental harm classification — the reason 'grandma's borax' is banned across much of Europe while sold freely in US grocery aisles.

Sodium Tetraborate.rule: US: EPA allows in household products; no federal repro restriction; OSHA GHS labels H360 but does not ban consumer sale.
Sodium Tetraborate.reason: Textbook catch-up case: same hazard classification on both sides of the Atlantic, different regulatory outcome.

Trichloroisocyanuric Acid.rule: EU — restricted in certain consumer uses; strong oxidizer handling rules.
Trichloroisocyanuric Acid.reason: Oxidizer (H271) + chlorinated byproduct formation (chlorine gas in misuse).

Ethanolamine.rule: EU Cosmetics Reg. — diethanolamine (DEA) banned outright (2004); monoethanolamine (MEA) restricted with nitrosamine safeguards; CLP classifies MEA H312/H332.
Ethanolamine.reason: Occupational asthma documented in cleaning-product formulation workers; nitrosamine contamination concern in amine-based formulas under acidic conditions.

DMDM Hydantoin.rule: EU Cosmetics Reg. Annex V, Entry 33 — allowed as preservative up to 0.6%, but must be labeled "releases formaldehyde" if formaldehyde released exceeds 0.001% (10 ppm) per Reg. 2022/1181.
DMDM Hydantoin.reason: Formaldehyde is a Category 1B carcinogen and skin sensitizer. DMDM Hydantoin releases formaldehyde to preserve products. EU tightened labeling threshold from 0.05% to 0.001% in 2022 to protect formaldehyde-sensitive consumers.

DMDM Hydantoin.rule: No federal labeling requirement for formaldehyde releasers. FDA does not regulate preservative labeling beyond ingredient disclosure. Products containing DMDM Hydantoin are sold without formaldehyde warning.
DMDM Hydantoin.reason: US regulatory gap: formaldehyde itself is banned in cosmetics (rarely used directly), but formaldehyde-releasing preservatives are common and unlabeled. Consumers with formaldehyde allergy have no way to identify risk.

Formaldehyde releaser (paraformaldehyde.rule: Commission Implementing Decision (EU) 2026/599 — Not approved as active substance for PT6 biocides (in-can preservatives). Products containing it must be withdrawn or reformulated.
Formaldehyde releaser (paraformaldehyde.reason: Formaldehyde-releasing preservative failed EU BPR approval for product-type 6. EU requires reformulation with approved alternatives.

Formaldehyde.rule: REACH Annex XVII Entry 77 — Indoor articles must not emit formaldehyde above 0.062 mg/m³ (furniture/wood) or 0.080 mg/m³ (other articles). Applies to furniture, wood-based products, foams, textiles, toys, electrical appliances.
Formaldehyde.reason: Formaldehyde classified as carcinogen (CLP). EU set strict indoor emission limits while US has no comparable federal standard.

1,4-Dioxane.rule: New York State ban: 1,4-dioxane in cleaning/personal care products capped at 1 ppm (effective Dec 2023). California requires disclosure at >1 ppm. No US federal restriction.
1,4-Dioxane.reason: Common contaminant in ethoxylated surfactants. Probable human carcinogen (IARC 2B). State-level action where federal has none.

1,4-Dioxane.rule: EU REACH 2026 Restrictions Roadmap lists certain uses of 1,4-dioxane for potential future restriction under REACH Annex XVII. Not yet adopted; under evaluation.
1,4-Dioxane.reason: Probable human carcinogen. Contaminant in ethoxylated surfactants used in cleaning products. EU considering restriction while US has only state-level limits.

Methylchloroisothiazolinone.rule: EU Cosmetics Reg. Annex V: the CMIT/MIT (3:1) mixture is banned in leave-on cosmetics; permitted only in rinse-off products at 15 ppm. CMIT alone may not be used in cosmetics at all.
Methylchloroisothiazolinone.reason: Contact-allergy epidemic — CMIT/MIT (trade name Kathon) became one of the most frequent causes of occupational and consumer allergic contact dermatitis, especially in cleaners and personal care. The rinse-off restriction followed sustained patch-test evidence.

Methylchloroisothiazolinone.rule: EU CLP classifies CMIT as H314 (corrosive), H317 (skin sensitizer), H400/H410 (very toxic to aquatic life). No equivalent US federal restriction in cleaning products.
Methylchloroisothiazolinone.reason: Both human sensitization and aquatic toxicity drive the EU classification; CMIT is acutely toxic to aquatic organisms at very low concentrations, which matters because cleaners go down the drain.

Methylchloroisothiazolinone.rule: No US federal ban or ppm cap for CMIT/MIT in household cleaning products. It remains a common in-can preservative in US carpet cleaners, detergents and hard-surface cleaners.
Methylchloroisothiazolinone.reason: US regulation of isothiazolinone preservatives in cleaning products is largely absent, so the same chemistry restricted in EU leave-on products is routine in US cleaners.

Butylphenyl Methylpropional.rule: EU Cosmetics Regulation Annex II — BMHCA (Lilial) classified CMR 1B (Repr. 1B) by Delegated Reg. (EU) 2020/1182; added to the prohibited list by Commission Reg. (EU) 2021/1902, applying from 1 March 2022. Note: the ban covers cosmetics — SCCS documentation records BMHCA is also used in household cleaners and detergents, which the cosmetics ban does not reach.
Butylphenyl Methylpropional.reason: CMR 1B (reprotoxic) classification; SCCS found it not safe as a fragrance ingredient under aggregate exposure.

Butylphenyl Methylpropional.rule: No federal restriction on BMHCA in cleaning products; no state ban identified. Still disclosed as a fragrance component in US detergents.
Butylphenyl Methylpropional.reason: Illustrates the transatlantic gap: a CMR fragrance removed from EU cosmetics remains permitted in US consumer products.

watchlist.name: Triclosan
watchlist.rule: EU banned in cosmetics. US FDA banned OTC antibacterial soaps 2016 — but it remains in some consumer products; the ban took 40+ years to catch up.
watchlist.reason: Endocrine disruption (thyroid), bacterial resistance, aquatic toxicity.

watchlist.name: Nonylphenol Ethoxylates
watchlist.rule: EU banned in cleaning products. US: EPA restricts industrial use only; consumer cleaning products can still contain them.

watchlist.name: Phosphates (detergents)
watchlist.rule: EU banned phosphates in laundry detergent (2013) and dishwasher detergent (2017). US: no federal ban; a few state-level limits.
watchlist.reason: Eutrophication — algal blooms and dead zones in waterways.

watchlist.name: Parabens (propyl/butyl)
watchlist.rule: EU banned propyl/butyl parabens in leave-on cosmetics for under-3s; ongoing endocrine review. US: allowed without age restriction.
watchlist.reason: Weak estrogenic activity; endocrine disruption concerns.

watchlist.name: Formaldehyde
watchlist.rule: EU banned in cosmetics (Annex II). US: no federal cosmetics ban; some states restrict.

watchlist.name: Titanium Dioxide (powder)
watchlist.rule: EU classified Carcinogen 1B by inhalation (2020); banned as food additive 2022. US: allowed in food and cosmetics.

watchlist.name: Microplastics (intentionally added)
watchlist.rule: EU banned intentionally-added microplastics (phased 2023–2035). US: state-level only.
watchlist.reason: Persistence and bioaccumulation; cleaning products with plastic scrubbing particles affected.

watchlist.name: Talc (asbestos-contaminated)
watchlist.rule: EU tightens asbestos-in-talc limits; ongoing litigation. US: FDA testing program, no ban.
watchlist.reason: Asbestos contamination/possible carcinogenicity; talc-based cleaning powders affected.

watchlist.name: 1,4-Dioxane
watchlist.rule: EU REACH 2026 Restrictions Roadmap lists certain uses of 1,4-dioxane for potential restriction. Not yet adopted but under evaluation. US: NY State banned 1,4-dioxane in cleaning/personal care products above 1 ppm (effective 2023); CA requires disclosure above 1 ppm.
watchlist.reason: 1,4-dioxane is a common contaminant in ethoxylated surfactants (SLES, etc.) used in dish soaps and detergents. Probable human carcinogen (IARC 2B). EU considering restriction; US has state-level action but no federal ban.
